Scaling Test-Time Compute for Agentic Coding

Joongwon (Daniel) Kim Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs Affiliation: University of Washington    Winnie Yang Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs Affiliation: New York University    Kelvin Niu Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Hongming Zhang Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Yun Zhu Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Eryk Helenowski Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Ruan Silva Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Zhengxing Chen Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Srini Iyer Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Manzil Zaheer Affiliation: Google DeepMind Work done while at Meta.    Daniel Fried Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Hannaneh Hajishirzi Affiliation: University of Washington    Sanjeev Arora Affiliation: Princeton University Work done while at Meta.    Gabriel Synnaeve Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Ruslan Salakhutdinov Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Work done while at Meta.    Anirudh Goyal Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs
Abstract

Test-time scaling has become a powerful way to improve large language models. However, existing methods are best suited to short, bounded outputs that can be directly compared, ranked or refined. Long-horizon coding agents violate this premise: each attempt produces an extended trajectory of actions, observations, errors, and partial progress taken by the agent. In this setting, the main challenge is no longer generating more attempts, but representing prior experience in a form that can be effectively selected from and reused. We propose a test-time scaling framework for agentic coding based on compact representations of rollout trajectories. Our framework converts each rollout into a structured summary that preserves its salient hypotheses, progress, and failure modes while discarding low-signal trace details. This representation enables two complementary forms of inference-time scaling. For parallel scaling, we introduce Recursive Tournament Voting (RTV), which recursively narrows a population of rollout summaries through small-group comparisons. For sequential scaling, we adapt Parallel-Distill-Refine (PDR) to the agentic setting by conditioning new rollouts on summaries distilled from prior attempts. Our method consistently improves the performance of frontier coding agents across SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0. For example, by using our method Claude-4.5-Opus improves from 70.9% →\rightarrow 77.6% on SWE-Bench Verified (mini-SWE-agent) and 46.9% →\rightarrow 59.1% on Terminal-Bench v2.0 (Terminus 1). Our results suggest that test-time scaling for long-horizon agents is fundamentally a problem of representation, selection, and reuse.

1 Introduction

Test-time scaling has become a major driver of progress in large language models  (OpenAI, 2024; Anthropic, 2025; Google, 2026; Feng et al., 2026). Rather than treating a model as a one-shot predictor, one can allocate additional inference-time compute to sample multiple candidates, aggregate or compare them, or refine later attempts using information from earlier ones  (Wang et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023; Snell et al., 2024; Madaan et al., 2025). This paradigm has proven effective in domains such as mathematical reasoning and single-turn code generation, where model outputs are compact enough to be manipulated directly in context  (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Zhuang et al., 2026; Venkatraman et al., 2025).

However, agentic coding introduces a distinct regime from such existing domains. To solve agentic coding tasks, instead of producing a single bounded completion, the model interacts with an external environment over many steps: reading files, editing code, inspecting logs, executing commands, and responding to intermediate failures. Each attempt therefore produces a long trajectory rather than a short response. These trajectories contain useful signal, but they also contain noisy, verbose details, and are difficult to compare or reuse directly (Xiao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Ehrlich et al., 2025; Antoniades et al., 2024; Ahmed et al., 2025). As a result, standard test-time scaling methods do not transfer cleanly to long-horizon agents.

In this work, we argue that the central bottleneck in scaling agentic coding is representation. To scale test-time compute effectively, inference should operate not on raw trajectories, but on their compact representations. We therefore summarize each rollout into a structured artifact that captures its key hypotheses, decisions, progress, and failure modes while omitting low-value trace detail (Lindenbauer et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025). These summaries become the interface through which prior attempts can be selected from and reused.

We apply these artifacts along two orthogonal dimensions of test-time scaling. First, we explore the parallel dimension (Kang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025) and introduce Recursive Tournament Voting (RTV) to select the strongest attempt from a population of rollouts without access to ground-truth outcomes (Section 2.3). Second, we explore the sequential dimension (Qu et al., 2024; Ding and Zhang, 2026; Zhuang et al., 2026) and adapt Parallel-Distill-Refine (PDR; Madaan et al. (2025)) to agentic coding by executing new rollouts conditioned on compact summaries distilled from prior rollouts (Section 2.4).

We perform a set of preliminary experiments to formulate our inference scaling method. First, we find that structured summaries outperform raw agentic trajectories as objects of comparison during parallel aggregation, showing that bounded summaries are a better substrate for rollout selection than full interaction logs. We also observe that recursive selections from small groups outperform flatter selections from large groups (Section 3.2.1). Moreover, we find that sequential refinement functions better by conditioning new rollouts on multiple prior summaries instead of a single prior attempt. We further observe that the quality of the refinement context is strongly related with the performance of the subsequent rollouts (Section 3.2.2).

Building on these results, we combine RTV and PDR into a unified test-time scaling recipe for agentic coding. Our recipe consistently improves over single-attempt baselines across frontier LLMs {Claude-4.5-Opus, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5-0825} and agentic coding benchmarks {SWE-Bench Verified, Terminal-Bench v2.0}. Using our method, on SWE-Bench Verified, Claude-4.5-Opus improves from 70.9% to 77.6% and Gemini-3.1-Pro from 72.3% to 76.6%, and on Terminal-Bench v2.0, Claude-4.5-Opus improves from 46.9% to 59.1% and Gemini-3.1-Pro from 52.5% to 64.8% (Section 3.3). Moreover, our method allows agents to aggregate and refine their solutions to successfully complete tasks that were not previously solvable within 16 initial rollouts (Appendix D), such as Claude-4.5-Opus solving gpt2-codegolf and Gemini-3.1-Pro solving large-scale-text-editing in Terminal-Bench v2.0 (Appendix F.2). Our results suggest that scaling long-horizon agentic systems depend not only on stronger base models, but also on high-quality trajectory representations and robust inference techniques.

Our contributions are threefold:

  1. 1.

    We identify the representation of prior agent experience as a central scientific bottleneck in inference-time scaling for long-horizon agentic coding through a series of targeted experiments.

  2. 2.

    We propose a unified framework in which compact structured rollout summaries serve as the interface for both parallel aggregation and sequential refinement, instantiated through RTV and agentic PDR.

  3. 3.

    We show empirically that this representation-centric approach yields strong gains across challenging agentic coding benchmarks across frontier models.

Taken together, these results suggest a simple view of the problem: for long-horizon agents, inference-time scaling is fundamentally a problem of representation, selection, and reuse.

2 Methodology

2.1 Problem Formulation

We scale test-time compute for agentic coding tasks, where a language model must solve a coding problem by interacting with an external bash environment over multiple steps. Given an agentic coding problem PinP_{\text{in}}, an agent ΠLM\Pi_{\text{LM}} produces a rollout ℛ\mathcal{R}, a trajectory consisting of a series of interleaved pairs of actions 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i} taken in the bash environment ℰ\mathcal{E}, and the associated observation 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i} returned by the terminal upon executing the agent’s action in ℰ\mathcal{E}, for a given step index ii. Each action consists of (1) the agent’s thought 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} which details the agent’s cognitive process, and (2) one or more bash commands ℬi={b1,…,b|ℬi|}\mathcal{B}_{i}=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{|\mathcal{B}_{i}|}\} to be executed in the terminal, generated by ΠLM\Pi_{\text{LM}}. Denoting the context accumulated from the previous step i−1i-1 as 𝒞i−1\mathcal{C}_{i-1} and the action generation prompt as 𝒫action\mathcal{P}_{\text{action}}, we have:

𝒜i=(𝒯i,ℬi)=ΠLM​[𝒫action​(Pin,𝒞i−1)]\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{i}=(\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{B}_{i})=\Pi_{\text{LM}}\left[\mathcal{P}_{\text{action}}(P_{\text{in}};\mathcal{C}_{i-1})\right] (1)

After parsing and executing the agent’s bash command in the environment ℰ\mathcal{E}, we gather the observation 𝒪i\mathcal{O}_{i} consisting of both the expected outputs and unexpected error messages:

𝒪i=ℰ⁡(𝒞i−1,ℬi)\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{i}=\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{C}_{i-1};\mathcal{B}_{i}) (2)

We then update ΠLM\Pi_{\text{LM}}’s context 𝒞i−1\mathcal{C}_{i-1} by appending the (action, observation) pair for step ii.

𝒞i=[𝒞i−1;(𝒜i,𝒪i)]\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{i}=[\mathcal{C}_{i-1};(\mathcal{A}_{i},\mathcal{O}_{i})] (3)

Our goal is to improve performance by scaling the number of rollouts rather than the number of tokens in a single generation. We treat a rollout as the primary scaling unit since it interleaves model outputs with observations, making token-level scaling difficult to interpret consistently across steps. Refer to Appendix F for examples of agentic coding rollout trajectories. We scale our rollouts along two orthogonal dimensions:

  • •

    Parallel scaling: execute multiple rollouts in separate containers and run selection.

  • •

    Sequential scaling: execute new sets of rollouts in freshly initialized containers while conditioning on information extracted from earlier attempts.

2.2 Rollout Summaries as Reusable Representations

A rollout trajectory is typically too long and noisy to compare or reuse directly. While it contains useful signal such as promising diagnoses, partial fixes or failure modes, it also contains low-signal detail such as repeated terminal output or dead-end local explorations (Xiao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Ehrlich et al., 2025). Given a rollout ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i}, we therefore first convert it into a compact, structured summary:

Si=ΠLM​[𝒫sum​(ℛi)]\displaystyle S_{i}=\Pi_{\mathrm{LM}}\!\left[\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{sum}}(\mathcal{R}_{i})\right] (4)

where 𝒫sum\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{sum}} is a summarization prompt. These summaries serve as the common interface for both components of our framework. In the parallel setting, they provide bounded objects over which multiple rollouts can be compared. In the sequential setting, they provide reusable context that can guide future rollouts without replaying full interaction histories in the previous-iteration rollouts. Refer to Appendix G for examples of the compact, structured summaries generated by ΠLM\Pi_{\mathrm{LM}}.

2.3 Parallel Selection via Recursive Tournament Voting

We first study the parallel dimension of inference-time scaling. Suppose we execute NN parallel, independent rollouts with ΠLM\Pi_{\mathrm{LM}} for the given agentic coding problem PinP_{\text{in}}:

𝒫0={ℛ1,…,ℛN}\mathcal{P}_{0}=\{\mathcal{R}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{R}_{N}\}

Our goal is to select the highest-quality rollout possible without access to any ground-truth outcomes, test cases or test samples. Note that for agentic coding tasks such as SWE-Bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) and Terminal-Bench v2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026) that involve binary pass or fail metrics, the upper bound of the post-aggregation pass@1 score is the pass@N score, where the selection matches oracle performance.

We introduce Recursive Tournament Voting (RTV) to perform this selection in three stages. Refer to Figure 2 for a visual overview of RTV:

  1. 1.

    Execute NN parallel rollouts.

  2. 2.

    Summarize each rollout into a compact, structured summary.

  3. 3.

    Recursively compare summaries in small groups until a single rollout remains.

After generating summaries {S1,…,SN}\{S_{1},\ldots,S_{N}\}, RTV executes stage 3 as a recursive procedure consisting of multiple rounds indexed with rr, where each round reduces a population of rollouts into a subset by dividing the population into groups of size GG and selecting a rollout from each group. More formally, for each round rr, RTV begins with a population of N(r)N^{(r)} remaining rollouts such that N(0)=NN^{(0)}=N. Within each group indexed by jj, RTV applies a comparison prompt 𝒫comp\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{comp}} and aggregates VV comparison votes to select one summary:

gj(r)=argmaxg∈{1,…,G}∑v=1V[ΠLM[𝒫comp(Pin;S(j,1)(r),…,S(j,G)(r))]=g],\displaystyle g_{j}^{(r)}=\arg\max_{g\in\{1,\ldots,G\}}\sum_{v=1}^{V}\mathds{1}\!\left[\Pi_{\mathrm{LM}}\!\left[\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{comp}}(P_{\mathrm{in}};S_{(j,1)}^{(r)},\ldots,S_{(j,G)}^{(r)})\right]=g\right], (5)

where S(j,g)(r)S_{(j,g)}^{(r)} denotes the gg-th summary in group jj at round rr.

The selected rollouts form the population for the next round:

𝒫r+1={ℛk|k=(j−1)​G+gj(r)​ for ​j∈{1,…,⌈|𝒫r|G⌉}}.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{r+1}=\left\{\mathcal{R}_{k}\;\middle|\;k=(j-1)G+g_{j}^{(r)}\text{ for }j\in\left\{1,\ldots,\left\lceil\frac{|\mathcal{P}_{r}|}{G}\right\rceil\right\}\right\}. (6)

After iterating Eqs. 5 and 6, RTV selects the final remaining rollout as its output.

2.4 Sequential reuse via Parallel-Distill-Refine

We next study the sequential dimension of inference-time scaling. Here, the objective is to improve future rollouts using information extracted from earlier ones.

To implement sequential refinement, we apply the random-KK variant of PDR to an agentic setting. We refer to the execution of parallel rollouts as an iteration, such that iteration-1 rollouts are refined from iteration-0 rollouts. Starting from an iteration-00 population

𝒫0={ℛ1,…,ℛN},\mathcal{P}_{0}=\{\mathcal{R}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{R}_{N}\},

we first summarize each rollout into {S1(0),…,SN(0)}\{S_{1}^{(0)},\ldots,S_{N}^{(0)}\} where each Si(t)S_{i}^{(t)} denotes the summary of the iith rollout of iteration tt. Then, for each rollout in the next iteration, we sample KK summaries from the previous iteration and use them as refinement context.

More formally, for rollout ii in iteration t+1t+1, let

Ji(t+1)⊆{1,…,N},|Ji(t+1)|=K\displaystyle J_{i}^{(t+1)}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\},\qquad|J_{i}^{(t+1)}|=K (7)

denote the set of indices associated with the selected summaries, and define the refinement context as a concatenation of the KK-selected summaries:

𝒞i(t+1)={Sj(t)∣j∈Ji(t+1)}\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{i}^{(t+1)}=\{S_{j}^{(t)}\mid j\in J_{i}^{(t+1)}\} (8)

PDR then executes each next-iteration rollout in a freshly initialized environment, generating the first action conditioned on both the original problem and this distilled prior experience:

𝒜i,0(t+1)=ΠLM​[𝒫action​(Pin,𝒞i(t+1))],\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{i,0}^{(t+1)}=\Pi_{\mathrm{LM}}\!\left[\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{action}}(P_{\mathrm{in}};\mathcal{C}_{i}^{(t+1)})\right], (9)

where 𝒜i,m(t+1)\mathcal{A}_{i,m}^{(t+1)} is the mmth action taken for the iith rollout in iteration t+1t+1. Subsequent actions follow the usual rollout dynamics from Eqs. 1 to 3, except with the refinement context added. As the original implementation of PDR selects its final rollout by executing a single rollout during its final iteration (Madaan et al., 2025), in this work we estimate its performance by averaging the scores of the NN final-iteration rollouts.

2.5 A unified pipeline: selection, then reuse, then selection

RTV and PDR address complementary aspects of inference-time scaling. RTV improves selection within a population of rollouts. PDR improves reuse of information across iterations. Our full recipe integrates these operators into a single pipeline. The full pipeline consists of:

  1. 1.

    Iteration 0: execute NN independent rollouts and perform summarization;

  2. 2.

    Select-KK: apply RTV to obtain a high-quality subset of KK summaries;

  3. 3.

    Iteration 1: execute NN fresh rollouts conditioned on the selected summaries;

  4. 4.

    Final RTV: apply RTV to the refined rollouts and return the final top-11 rollout.

In a way, we maintain a balance of exploitation and exploration – exploitation by narrowing down the search space to a subset of K<NK<N higher-quality rollouts using RTV, and exploration by using K>1K>1 rollouts to maintain diversity and cross-pollinating potentially diverse solution approaches for executing the next-iteration rollouts. Moreover, instead of performing a single rollout for the final iteration as done in vanilla PDR, we also opt to leverage the parallel selection capability in RTV to exploit the residual diversity among the refined rollouts and select the final rollout. Figure 3 illustrates the full pipeline of our PDR + RTV method.

3 Results and Analyses

We evaluate our method in three stages: (1) present our method ablations and design choices that motivate our framework, (2) report our main results, and (3) analyze the sequential & parallel dynamics of our method.

A consistent picture emerges from our experiments. First, compact structured summaries function as better interfaces than full rollout traces for both selection and reuse. Second, Recursive Tournament Voting (RTV) is effective at selecting among long-horizon agentic trajectories, and its benefits persist after refinement. Third, refinement contexts built from stronger rollouts leads to stronger next-iteration rollouts, indicating that the gains from sequential refinement are driven by the quality of the prior experience that is reused.

3.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate on two agentic coding benchmarks – SWE-Bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) and Terminal-Bench v2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026) – using Claude-4.5-Opus, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Flash and GPT-5-0825. Our main experiments in Section 3.3 use N=16N=16, T=2T=2, K=4K=4, G=2G=2, and V=8V=8. For SWE-Bench Verified, we evaluate on the full test set. For Terminal-Bench v2.0, we evaluate on 88 of the 89 tasks available to us. Refer to Appendix A for more details on the model capabilities, Appendix B for their head-to-head comparisons, and Appendix F.1 for examples of our rollout trajectories, for these benchmarks.

3.2 Method Ablations and Design Choices

We begin by presenting the ablations that motivate the final design of our framework. First, we study parallel aggregation in isolation. Then we turn to sequential refinement.

3.2.1 Parallel Aggregation Ablations

We first identify the best substrate for comparing agentic rollouts during RTV. A direct approach is to compare the full rollout traces {ℛ1,…,ℛN}\{\mathcal{R}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{R}_{N}\}. Alternatively, the rollouts can be represented as compact, structured summaries {𝒮1,…,𝒮N}\{\mathcal{S}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{N}\}. Figure 4 shows the result of our investigation on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0 using Claude-4.5-Sonnet and Gemini-3-Flash.

Across both models and both benchmarks, we find that using compact, structured summaries as representations consistently outperforms directly comparing full rollout trajectories – full trajectories are too long and noisy to serve as reliable objects of comparison, whereas bounded structured summaries preserve the decisive information while discarding low-signal detail. More specifically, as the tournament eliminates the “easier” pairs in the earlier rounds and are left with more difficult candidates that require attention to nuanced details for accurate selection, using compact summaries in the final round (Round 4 in Figure 4) provides a decisive advantage over full rollout traces as representations for selecting higher-quality rollouts.

We next investigate the architecture of RTV. A natural baseline is to load all NN summaries into context and perform a single comparison. Alternatively, our proposed RTV architecture decomposes the selection procedure into repeated smaller comparisons. Figure 5 reports the effect of varying the group size G∈{16,8,4,2}G\in\{16,8,4,2\} and the number of candidate comparison votes V∈{1,2,4,8,16}V\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}.

Figure 5 (Left) shows that smaller-group recursive comparison performs better than flatter selection schemes, with pairwise comparisons (G=2G=2) yielding the strongest results. This suggests that selecting among long-horizon trajectories is easier when decomposed into a sequence of local decisions rather than a single global ranking over many candidates. Meanwhile, Figure 5 (Right) shows that vote aggregation improves the reliability of these local decisions, with clear gains as VV increases and diminishing returns beginning around V=8V=8. These observations motivate our default RTV configuration of G=2G=2 and V=8V=8.

We then evaluate RTV as a standalone selection mechanism with N=16N=16, with the results in Figure 6. Across all five models, RTV improves performance over the average rollout in the initial population on both SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0, with the largest gains in Terminal-Bench v2.0. For example, Claude-4.5-Sonnet improves from 67.4%→73.6%67.4\%\rightarrow 73.6\% on SWE-Bench Verified and from 40.6%→54.6%40.6\%\rightarrow 54.6\% on Terminal-Bench v2.0. These results show that recursive selection over structured summaries is already a strong test-time scaling method in isolation, even without performing sequential refinement.

3.2.2 Sequential Refinement Ablations

We next probe our design choices for sequential refinement. First, we study the effects of the prior rollout composition in the refinement context on the next-iteration rollouts. Table 1 compares three methods on 100 SWE-Bench Verified tasks using Claude-4.5-Sonnet and Gemini-3.1-Pro: {single-rollout, random-KK, select-KK}-refinement. For single-rollout, we take NN parallel rollouts and refine each iteration-0 rollout by using its own structured summary to execute the associated iteration-1 rollout. For random-KK, we follow PDR and randomly sample KK previous summaries into the previous-iteration rollouts to provide as refinement context for executing each next-iteration rollout. For select-KK, we run RTV on the NN parallel rollouts via tournament voting until we obtain KK remaining rollouts. We use N=16N=16 rollouts for each iteration, and K=4K=4 prior rollouts for building the refinement context.

For building the refinement context, using KK=4 prior rollouts even via random selection clearly outperforms using a single prior rollout. For example, the average pass@1 score of Gemini-3.1-Pro improves only from 72.69%→73.75%72.69\%\rightarrow 73.75\% under single-rollout refinement, but improves from 72.69%→76.94%72.69\%\rightarrow 76.94\% under random-KK refinement. Moreover, selecting the KK=4 rollouts using RTV (select-KK) further improves performance, reaching 79.25%79.25\% for Gemini-3.1-Pro and 78.06%78.06\% for Claude-4.5-Sonnet during iteration 1.

Figure 7 provides a more detailed view by comparing the pass-count distributions under single-rollout and random-KK refinement. For both Claude-4.5-Sonnet and Gemini-3.1-Pro, the distribution under random-KK refinement shifts toward larger numbers of passing rollouts relative to single-rollout refinement. For example, using Claude-4.5-Sonnet with single rollout as refinement context yields 40/100 tasks with 16/16 passes, while with random-K rollout as refinement context it yields 51/100 such tasks. These results indicate that using multiple prior trajectories improves not only the mean but the full distribution of next-iteration outcomes.

We also study how the quality of the refinement context affects next-iteration rollouts. Table 2 stratifies the results for random-KK and select-KK refinement, based on how many of the KK=4 context rollouts succeed. The success rates of the iteration-1 rollouts increase monotonically with the success rate of the refinement context across both setups, rising from near-zero for 0/4 success-rate contexts to 97–99% for 4/4 success-rate contexts. It also shows that RTV yields more 4/4 passing rollouts than random selection, with 62 vs. 52.8 tasks for Claude-4.5-Sonnet and 71 vs. 58.5 tasks for Gemini-3.1-Pro. Figure 14 in Appendix C.1 visualizes the stratified pass rate distributions. The distributions shift rightward with increasing context pass rate for both Claude-4.5-Sonnet and Gemini-3.1-Pro, indicating that even small improvements in context quality translate into measurable performance gains in next-iteration rollouts. These results motivate our approach of combining RTV with PDR, so that the refinement context is constructed to be maximally informative.

3.3 Main Results

We now turn to the full PDR+RTV pipeline. Table 3 and Figure 1 summarize the performance of our full PDR+RTV recipe across our agentic coding benchmarks and frontier models.

On SWE-Bench Verified, our method yields consistent gains over the single-attempt baselines (Iter 0). In particular, the final RTV-selected candidate improves Claude-4.5-Opus from 70.94%→77.60%70.94\%\rightarrow 77.60\% (+6.66), Gemini-3.1-Pro from 72.25%→76.60%72.25\%\rightarrow 76.60\% (+4.35), Claude-4.5-Sonnet from 67.41%→75.60%67.41\%\rightarrow 75.60\% (+8.19), Gemini-3-Flash from 70.79%→76.00%70.79\%\rightarrow 76.00\% (+5.21), and GPT-5-0825 from 61.41%→69.80%61.41\%\rightarrow 69.80\% (+8.39). These improvements are visible in Figure 1 and reflect complementary contributions from (i) improved rollout quality after selecting the KK candidates and refining the rollouts (Iter 1), and (ii) an additional selection boost from the final RTV on top of the iteration-1 rollouts (Final).

On Terminal-Bench v2.0, we observe even larger absolute improvements, consistent with the benchmark’s higher variance and the importance of selecting among long-horizon trajectories. The final candidate improves Claude-4.5-Opus from 46.95%→59.09%46.95\%\rightarrow 59.09\% (+12.14), Gemini-3.1-Pro from 52.49%→64.77%52.49\%\rightarrow 64.77\% (+12.28), Claude-4.5-Sonnet from 40.62%→56.82%40.62\%\rightarrow 56.82\% (+16.20), Gemini-3-Flash from 37.93%→48.86%37.93\%\rightarrow 48.86\% (+10.93), and GPT-5-0825 from 31.32%→38.64%31.32\%\rightarrow 38.64\% (+7.32). Notably, RTV provides a substantial lift over the raw iteration-1 rollouts (e.g., 52.49% →\rightarrow 59.09% for Claude-4.5-Opus and 56.89% →\rightarrow 64.77% for Gemini-3.1-Pro), indicating that even after sequential refinement, there remains meaningful diversity among rollouts that can be exploited by parallel aggregation. Our method also helps coding agents to complete tasks that were not previously solvable within their 16 initial rollouts, as shown in Appendix D. As examples of new solution discovery behavior, Figures 21 and 22 in Appendix F.2 shows Claude-4.5-Opus solving gpt2-codegolf and Gemini-3.1-Pro solving large-scale-text-editing in Terminal-Bench v2.0 under the Terminus-1 scaffold.

Meanwhile, for our main experiments in SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0 we also measure the average number of steps taken by the agent for each iteration, both across all rollouts in each iteration and further divided into passing and failing rollouts. Table 4 shows the results of our analyses. Across both benchmarks and all of our models, iteration 1 rollouts take substantially fewer steps than iteration 0. For example, upon refinement Claude-4.5-Opus drops from 41.23 →\rightarrow 14.31 steps on SWE-Bench Verified and 24.43 →\rightarrow 12.14 steps on Terminal-Bench v2.0. Similarly, Gemini-3.1-Pro drops from 35.56 →\rightarrow 17.95 steps on SWE-Bench Verified and 21.57 →\rightarrow 10.95 steps on Terminal-Bench v2.0.

These results suggest that the refinement context helps agents navigate to solutions more directly, cutting down on the additional steps which would typically be used to understand the directory structure, explore file contents, try erroneous approaches and more, increasing the search efficiency. We also observe a consistent gap between the length of passing and failing trajectories within each iteration, with failing rollouts consuming more steps on average than the passing rollouts. This is expected, as (1) the failing rollouts are more likely associated with difficult problems that require a large number of steps to address, and (2) the agent would be more likely to make mistakes in failing rollouts which would trigger recovery actions that consume more steps. Refer to Appendix E for examples of refinement behavior while running PDR+RTV on our benchmarks.

4 Analysis

We now perform a deeper analysis of our PDR+RTV test-time scaling method across two dimensions: sequential refinement and parallel aggregation. First, we study sequential refinement dynamics: how the pass rate of each task transitions from iteration 0 to 1, and how the quality of the refinement context with the KK selected rollouts influences iteration-1 behavior and efficiency. Second, we study parallel aggregation dynamics: how recursive small-group comparisons in RTV translate rollout diversity into reliable final-candidate selection.

4.1 Sequential Refinement Dynamics

We next analyze how the rollout populations change from iteration 0 to iteration 1 under the full PDR+RTV pipeline. Figure 8 visualizes the pass-count transition matrices for each (benchmark, model) combination, where the benchmark is either SWE-Bench Verified (Top) or Terminal-Bench v2.0 (Bottom) and the model is one of {Claude-4.5-Opus, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Flash}. Each row corresponds to the number of passing rollouts out of N=16N=16 rollouts in iteration 0, and each column corresponds to the number of passing rollouts in iteration 1. The mass above the diagonal corresponds to tasks with improvements, while mass below corresponds to tasks with regressions. Across both SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0, the matrices exhibit a pronounced upward shift, indicating that sequential refinement improves the overall pass rates for a substantial fraction of tasks.

To better understand the factors leading to improved pass rates upon sequential refinement, for each task in our SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0 main experiments we bucket tasks by how many of the K=4K=4 iteration-0 rollouts selected into the refinement context are passing. Within each bucket, we then report the resulting iteration-1 pass@1 (along with the number of tasks in that bucket).

Table 5 reports the results of our analysis. Across all four models, the average pass@1 score of the iteration-1 rollouts increases sharply as the quality of the refinement context improves. For example, Claude-4.5-Opus scores 0.1% on tasks with 0 out of 4 passing rollouts in the refinement context, 33.4% on tasks with 1 out of 4 passing rollouts, 55.5% on tasks with 2 out of 4 passing rollouts, 85.4% on tasks with 3 out of 4 passing rollouts, and 99.2% on tasks with 4 out of 4 passing rollouts for SWE-Bench Verified. The same pattern holds for all other models, and also on Terminal-Bench v2.0. These results strongly indicate that selected prior experience directly drives next-iteration performance.

We also provide the pass count distribution shifts from iteration 0→10\rightarrow 1 across the four models for both SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0. Refer to Figures 9 and 10 for the pass count distribution shifts on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0, respectively. Across both SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0, the number of rollouts with 16/16 passes increases from iteration 0→10\rightarrow 1, because the transitions in the rightmost column in Figure 8 leverages the high-quality rollouts selected for the refinement context to achieve high refinement success rates. Meanwhile, we also observe an increase in the number of rollouts with 0/16 passes from iteration 0→10\rightarrow 1, associated with the transitions in the leftmost column in Figure 8. This is because, for parallel rollouts of low success rates, RTV often retains one or less successful candidates in its top-4 candidates, which as observed in Table 5, leads to next-iteration rollouts with high failure rates. As a result, we obtain a sharp, bimodal distribution of tasks for the iteration-1 rollouts, albeit with a much higher rate of increases in the first category of successful rollouts than increases in the second category of failing rollouts. For example, in Figure 9, during sequential refinement Claude-4.5-Opus increases the number of tasks with 16/16 passing rollouts from 209/500 to 350/500 (+141) in SWE-Bench Verified, while increasing the number of tasks with 0/16 passing rollouts from 73/500 to 94/500 (+21). Hence the average pass@1 score undergoes a net improvement from iteration 0→10\rightarrow 1, and this refinement dynamic sets up a favorable ground for a final round of RTV, as we investigate in the next section.

4.2 Parallel Aggregation Dynamics

We next study the parallel aggregation dynamics occurring during the execution of our PDR+RTV method. In particular, we investigate how RTV continues to improve performance even after sequential refinement. Given T=2T=2 iterations, there are two occurrences of RTV – the first instance after the completion of the iteration-0 rollouts, which performs tournament voting up to the top-4 candidates, and the second instance after the completion of the iteration-1 rollouts, which performs tournament voting up to the final candidate. While we only use the top-4 candidates for the first instance of RTV in our final method, we still run it to the final candidate for a comprehensive analysis of both RTV instances. To analyze both instances of RTV, we first monitor two evaluation metrics across the tournament rounds:

  1. 1.

    Average pass@1: This metric computes the pass@1 score of the candidates remaining in each tournament round. It generally increases over the tournament rounds as ΠLM\Pi_{\text{LM}} selects a higher proportion of successful rollouts over failing rollouts during each round.

  2. 2.

    pass@N: This metric computes the pass@N score of the candidates remaining in each tournament round. It decreases or stays the same over the tournament rounds as ΠLM\Pi_{\text{LM}} selects failing rollouts for some groups in each round, which may lead to only failing rollouts remaining for those groups.

Figures 11 and 12 show the results of our analyses performed for SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0, respectively. Each figure contains results spanning over the four models in {Claude-4.5-Opus, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Flash}. The blue lines in the first row report the average pass@1 scores across tournament rounds, while the orange lines in the second row report the pass@N scores, for both instances of RTV performed after iterations 0 and 1.

We make the following observations across both benchmarks and all frontier models. First, the second instance of RTV over the iteration-1 rollouts still provides improvements via parallel aggregation, albeit at a smaller rate than the rate of increase for the first instance of RTV over the iteration-0 rollouts. This is because of the distributions observed in Figures 9 and 10, where the number of tasks with mixed pass/fail test outcomes significantly decreases, leaving less room for improvement via tournament-based selection. Second, while the pass@N scores of the iteration-1 rollouts begin at lower points than the iteration-0 rollouts as some successful rollouts are incorrectly removed by the first instance of RTV, the pass@N scores of the iteration-1 rollouts converge to a higher final pass@1 score than those of the iteration-0 rollouts. This is because, as described above, some of the tasks regress to producing 0/16 successful rollouts in iteration 1, and this leaves a set of tasks with iteration-1 rollouts that are more convenient on average for RTV to operate over.

Moreover, we measure the accuracy of the groupwise comparisons performed during both instances of RTV across all of our experiments. Within each instance of RTV, across the tournament rounds we extract all groups containing both successful and failing rollouts, and we measure the selection accuracy, i.e. the ratio of groups from which a successful rollout is selected. In other words, we measure the performance of ΠLM\Pi_{\text{LM}} as a LLM-as-a-Judge in terms of how accurately it selects a successful rollout during each groupwise comparison.

Table 6 shows the results of our analyses. Note that the group selection accuracies in Table 6 should not be interpreted as a controlled, head-to-head comparison across judges/models. Each judge is applied to different sets of candidate rollouts produced by different generator models (i.e., itself), and it makes decisions based on summaries that are themselves generated from those rollouts. As a result, differences in the selection accuracies not only involve the judge’s decision quality, but also (i) the difficulty and diversity of the underlying rollout pools, and (ii) the informativeness of the corresponding summaries. Nevertheless, we make several observations. First, ΠLM\Pi_{\text{LM}} performs more accurate rollout selections amongst Terminal-Bench v2.0 rollouts than SWE-Bench Verified rollouts. This gap likely reflects that SWE-Bench Verified rollouts require judging subtle code diffs and hidden test outcomes from partial summaries, whereas Terminal-Bench v2.0 rollouts expose more directly verifiable command–output evidence, making successful trajectories easier for the judge to identify. Second, there is room for improving the groupwise comparison accuracies – for example, Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves the lowest accuracy as a judge11 1 We have experienced many API failure rates with Gemini-3.1-Pro during our final RTV experiments due to infrastructure issues, which may be related to its abnormally lower success rate as a judge. which results in the lowest improvement from the average pass@1 of its iteration-1 rollouts (76.16%) to its final pass@1 (76.60%, +0.44%). We expect that training ΠLM\Pi_{\text{LM}} to make better group-level rollout selections via SFT or RL, or even deploying a dedicated judge for tournament voting, would significantly improve the performance of RTV in our setup.

5 Conclusion

We propose a new inference-time scaling method for agentic coding, a setting in which each attempt is not a short completion but a long interactive trajectory of reasoning, actions, observations, and partial progress. For agentic tasks, we find that leveraging additional computation is useful only if the information produced by prior attempts can be exposed in a bounded form that later computation can reliably compare and reuse.

Our central claim is that the key bottleneck of leveraging inference-time compute for long-horizon tasks is the representation of prior experience. For agentic coding tasks, we address this bottleneck by converting each rollout into a compact, structured summary which functions as an interface for two complementary forms of test-time scaling. For parallel aggregation, we introduce Recursive Tournament Voting (RTV), which recursively selects successful rollouts by aggregating small-group comparisons of the structured summaries. For sequential refinement, we adapt Parallel-Distill-Refine (PDR) to the agentic setting by conditioning fresh rollouts upon summaries distilled from prior attempts. Combining these two operators yields a simple unified pipeline that balances exploitation by refining high-quality rollouts and exploration by executing multiple parallel rollouts.

Across different frontier LLMs {Claude-4.5-Opus, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5-0825} and challenging agentic coding benchmarks {SWE-Bench Verified, Terminal-Bench v2.0}, our framework consistently improves over single-attempt baselines. Our analyses further show that these gains are not simply explained by more compute – we find that (1) structured summaries outperform raw trajectories as comparison inputs, (2) refinement contexts with higher-quality summaries lead to stronger next-iteration rollouts, and (3) a final RTV stage continues to add value even after refinement by exploiting residual rollout diversity. Moreover, we find that sequential refinement via agentic PDR also improves the efficiency of the next-iteration rollouts, completing the same task using about 50% less steps while increasing their success rates. Taken together, these results support a simple view: for long-horizon agents, test-time scaling works when prior experience is transformed into representations that support both selection and reuse.

A natural direction for future work is to extend this framework beyond textual rollout summaries to persistent external artifacts. In our current setting, prior experience is reused through compact summaries provided to fresh rollouts in newly initialized environments. A richer formulation would allow agents to retain and build upon persistent workspace state across attempts, including notes, partial patches, derived tests, debugging scripts, and reusable tools constructed by the agent itself. This would move inference-time scaling from reusing descriptions of prior experience to reusing the artifacts produced by prior experience. An important open question is then how to represent, select, refine, and maintain such persistent artifacts so that agents can accumulate useful external state without being overwhelmed by stale or low-value information.

Appendix A Rollout statistics [return to table of contents]

We compute statistics regarding the rollouts performed by all of our models {Claude-4.5-Opus, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5-0825} for our main experiments and share the results in Tables 7 and 8 for SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0, respectively.

We measure, for each iteration of our main experiment, (1) the average pass@1 score, (2) the pass@16 score (NN=16), and (3) the number of tasks which contain mixed passing and failing rollouts for the given iteration. Note that for SWE-Bench Verified we use the bash-only mini-SWE-agent harness, and for Terminal-Bench v2.0 we use the Terminus 1 harness.

We find that Gemini-3.1-Pro performs the best across both benchmarks, closely followed by Claude-4.5-Opus. Gemini-3-Flash outperforms Claude-4.5-Sonnet in SWE-Bench Verified but Claude-4.5-Sonnet outperforms Gemini-3-Flash in Terminal-Bench v2.0. GPT-5-0825 performs the worst, which is expected given its earlier release date compared to the others.

Appendix B Model comparisons [return to table of contents]

We compare the capabilities of the frontier language models used in our experiments, {Claude-4.5-Opus, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5-0825}, for both SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0. To this end, for each pair of models (MiM_{i}, MjM_{j}) we compute the number of tasks where given NN=16 parallel rollouts in iteration 0, MiM_{i} is able to succeed in at least one of its rollouts while MjM_{j} fails all of its rollouts.

Figure 13 visualizes the results of our investigation. We find that Gemini-3.1-Pro is overall the most competitive across both benchmarks in terms of win rates, closely followed by Claude-4.5-Opus. Gemini-3-Flash has slightly better win rates than Claude-4.5-Sonnet on SWE-Bench Verified but does worse than Claude-4.5-Sonnet on Terminal-Bench v2.0. GPT-5-0825 is the least competitive, which is expected given its earlier release date than the other models. Meanwhile, we also observe that smaller models from the same family struggle more to outperform their larger counterparts, such as Gemini-3-Flash winning over Gemini-3.1-Pro for only 10/500 tasks on SWE-Bench Verified and only 1/88 tasks on Terminal-Bench v2.0. We observe similar patterns with Claude-4.5-Sonnet and Claude-4.5-Opus, but not as pronounced as the Gemini family of models.

Appendix C Sequential refinement dynamics [return to table of contents]

We provide additional results for the sequential refinement analyses performed for our PDR+RTV main experiments, as done in Section 4.1.

C.1 Context quality analysis

In Section 3.2.2, Table 2 shows the effect of refinement context management on the performance of the next-iteration rollouts, comparing random-KK refinement with select-KK (RTV) refinement, by stratifying the tasks by the number of passing rollouts in the context windows. The results in the table show that the select-KK refinement yields more refinement contexts with all-passing rollouts, which contributes to the improved average pass@1 score compared to the rollouts executed via random-KK refinement.

In Figure 14 we explore this further and visualize the task-level pass rate distribution of 100 randomly-sampled tasks from SWE-Bench Verified, for Claude-4.5-Sonnet and Gemini-3.1-Pro. Again, for each model we stratify the tasks by the number of passing rollouts in the refinement context, but this time we measure the per-bucket distribution of tasks in terms of their average iteration-1 pass rates.

Appendix D New solution discoveries [return to table of contents]

We identify the tasks which the frontier models used in our experiments, {Claude-4.5-Opus, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5-0825}, are initially unable to solve across its NN=16 parallel rollouts, but are able to solve upon performing the select-KK refinement during our PDR+RTV method. In other words, despite being provided a refinement context with the summaries of all-failing rollouts, the models produce next-iteration rollouts that pass all test cases. Tables 9 and 10 list the task IDs for each model that discover new solutions upon refinement for SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0, respectively.

We observe that despite there being almost six times as many tasks in SWE-Bench Verified compared to Terminal-Bench v2.0, there are 13 tasks with 0→\rightarrow1 improvement capabilities in Terminal-Bench v2.0 across all models compared to 5 tasks for SWE-Bench Verified.

Moreover, we analyze whether the tasks improving from fail →\rightarrow pass from iteration 0 to 1 had already been solved by other models during their iteration-0 rollouts. Tables 11 and 12 show the results of our analysis across all the frontier models on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench v2.0, respectively.

We find that all the Terminal-Bench v2.0 tasks that Claude-4.5-Opus can self-improve are already solved by Gemini-3.1-Pro in at least one of its iteration-0 rollouts. At the same time, all but one of the Terminal-Bench v2.0 tasks that Gemini-3.1-Pro can self-improve are already solved either by Claude-4.5-Opus or Claude-4.5-Sonnet in at least one of their iteration-0 rollouts. Interestingly, the mcmc-sampling-stan task self-improved by Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Flash and GPT-5-0825 are originally only solved by Gemini-3.1-Pro. Finally, while none of our models are able to solve large-scale-text-editing initially, Gemini-3.1-Pro can leverage PDR+RTV to execute a successful rollout during iteration 1.

Appendix E PDR + RTV qualitative examples [return to table of contents]

We present excerpts of several example rollout trajectories generated using our PDR+RTV method, where the agent leverages the structured summaries of previous rollouts, synthesizes common approaches and reconciles conflicting details in order to execute a new, successful rollout. Figure 15 shows an example of Claude-4.5-Opus solving the django_django-13033 task in SWE-Bench Verified. Figure 16 shows an example of Gemini-3.1-Pro solving the sympy_sympy-17318 task in SWE-Bench Verified. Figure 17 shows an example of Claude-4.5-Opus solving the sparql-university task in Terminal-Bench v2.0. Figure 18 shows an example of Claude-4.5-Sonnet solving the sqlite-db-truncate task in Terminal-Bench v2.0.

Figure 15 contains an excerpt of a rollout trajectory generated by Claude-4.5-Opus for completing the django_django-13033 task in SWE-Bench Verified. In Step 1, the agent draws on all four previous attempts’ analyses, synthesizing the commonly identified root cause (line 730 in find_ordering_name), the diagnosis that the name is the full path instead of the last piece, and the fix (pieces[-1]). Moreover, it does not repeat the extensive exploration performed by all four previous rollouts but rather proceeds directly to the precise file and line number based on the information from the previous summaries. In Step 2, the agent refers back to the synthesized findings from the prior rollouts by using the phrase “According to the analysis”. It applies both substitutions (name → pieces[-1] in both the attname check and the ‘pk’ check), which matches the approach from two of the previous rollouts, whose sed commands replaced both occurrences. It also uses the same sed command used by two previous rollouts, directly reusing the working fix pattern. Finally, in Step 5, the agent preemptively installs all three Python dependencies (asgiref, pytz, sqlparse) at once, in contrast to the four previous rollouts which all encountered ModuleNotFoundError.

Figure 16 contains an excerpt of a rollout trajectory generated by Gemini-3.1-Pro for completing the sympy_sympy-17318 task in SWE-Bench Verified. In Step 1, the agent mentions the previous findings about the call chain (split_surds → _split_gcd(*surds) → empty tuple → IndexError), which was traced by all four prior rollouts. Also, the phrase “agreed-upon fix from the successful parallel attempts” explicitly acknowledges consolidating the consensus from the summaries, where all four rollouts proposed the same guard clause in _split_gcd. Furthermore, the phrase “Another approach adds an early return in …” shows the refined rollout is aware of the divergence between attempts – one rollout modified split_surds with an early return, while another rollout additionally modified _sqrt_match. The refined rollout acknowledges both alternatives before choosing its final strategy. In Step 8, the agent directly refers to a specific finding from a prior attempt which discovered the TypeError in sqrt_biquadratic_denest. The refined rollout reproduces the exact same test to confirm the issue exists, rather than discovering it from scratch. In Step 9, the agent reasons about the TypeError to justify a two-file fix. Motivated by the discovery made by one of the previous rollouts, the refined rollout uses this understanding to justify why a second fix in _sqrt_match (returning [] when b == S.Zero) is necessary – which is exactly the two-file approach taken by one of the previous rollouts which was also the only passing prior rollout.

Figure 17 contains an excerpt of a rollout trajectory generated by Claude-4.5-Opus for completing the sparql-university task in Terminal-Bench v2.0. In Step 1, it explicitly states “Based on the analysis of 4 previous parallel attempts” and then enumerates four “Key insights from previous attempts.” Each insight maps to specific discoveries from the prior summaries – for example, it leverages an observation from a passing attempt that “the ¿10 students department doesn’t need to be in EU, just need to work in SOME EU department and SOME department with ¿10 students (they can be different)” and switches from a combined to a separate approach. In Step 4, the agent correctly synthesizes the differences in the approaches taken by previous attempts and selects the correct approach. While two of the failing previous attempts combined the EU check and ¿10 students check, producing incorrect results, another successful previous attempt independently discovered this separation by analyzing the test expectations. The refined rollout explicitly calls this out as a “Key insight” which is directly informed by the prior attempts’ divergent outcomes.

Figure 18 contains an excerpt of a rollout trajectory generated by Claude-4.5-Sonnet for completing the sqlite-db-truncate task in Terminal-Bench v2.0. The preamble in Step 1 draws on the four prior summaries and enumerates their shared findings. Moreover, the agent synthesizes the “key insights from all attempts”. It also resolves a critical conflict between the previous attempts about data types by choosing the interpretation taken by the successful attempts (“seems more accurate based on the SQLite serial type parsing”), the key technical distinction between the passing and failing rollouts. In Step 2, the agent directly references the approach taken by the successful previous attempts (“I will create a comprehensive Python script that properly parses the SQLite B-tree leaf page structure…”), skipping all dead ends from prior attempts to go directly to a complete SQLite B-tree leaf page parser. It produces the final working script in a single step.
